title: Fasting in children: signs of dehydration, when to break the fast immediately, and when to call emergency services

text_original: This unit draws on public health guidance pages accessed on 5 October 2026. We restated their facts in our own words rather than quoting their text: (1) NHS, “Dehydration”: children are more vulnerable to dehydration; symptoms include thirst, headache and dizziness, dark yellow strong-smelling urine, urinating less, lightheadedness, tiredness, a dry mouth, lips and tongue, and sunken eyes; drink fluids, starting with small sips and gradually increasing if vomiting, and avoid caffeinated drinks; seek urgent medical care now if the child seems unusually drowsy, dizziness on standing persists, urine is dark or reduced, breathing or heart rate is fast, or there are fewer tears; call emergency services or go to emergency care if dehydration is accompanied by blue, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue, cold skin, difficult or rapid breathing, confusion, or marked drowsiness and difficulty waking, as these may be signs of shock. (2) Saudi Ministry of Health, “Children and Ramadan”: make sure the child is ready and willing; do not have the child fast while ill and tired; introduce fasting gradually for young children; a child is not obliged to fast and must not be forced; watch for dehydration and low blood sugar during fasting; avoid heat, sun and exercise in the school playground; reduce tea and coffee because caffeine is a diuretic; praise and encourage the child. (3) Saudi Ministry of Health, “Ramadan Fasting and Dehydration”: children and people with chronic illnesses such as diabetes and kidney disease are among those most vulnerable to dehydration during fasting; symptoms include a very dry mouth, fatigue and lethargy, poor concentration, sleeping a lot, muscle cramps, dizziness and confusion, possibly progressing to fainting; anyone too dizzy to stand or confused should drink water immediately; someone who faints is laid on their back with feet raised until they regain consciousness, then given water; prevention includes water spread between iftar and suhoor, soup, water-rich fruits and vegetables such as watermelon and cucumber, reducing salt and caffeine, and avoiding the sun. (4) ramadan_family.json, “Fasting ladder”: fasting before puberty is practice, not an obligation; puberty rather than age makes fasting obligatory, and the details of its signs should be sought from scholars; signs to stop include dizziness, blurred vision, paleness or cold sweat, severe headache or persistent abdominal pain, vomiting, unusual drowsiness, severe lethargy or difficulty concentrating, very little or dark urine or a very dry mouth, and, before puberty, saying they cannot continue; break the fast immediately with water and a date or juice, then rest, praise without blame or comparison, and seek urgent medical care now for the NHS urgent signs of dehydration without waiting for improvement after breaking the fast; emergency signs include fainting or a seizure, confusion, unintelligible speech or difficulty waking, repeated vomiting preventing drinking, and, in a child with diabetes, any sign of low blood sugar such as trembling, sweating or confusion; call emergency services immediately, give nothing by mouth until fully conscious, and follow the diabetic child's doctor's low blood sugar plan; consult a doctor before any fasting for diabetes or a chronic illness such as kidney or heart disease, epilepsy or severe anemia, regular daytime medicine, severe thinness or delayed growth or weight gain, recent illness such as fever, diarrhea or vomiting, a history of an eating disorder or intense preoccupation with weight; after puberty, an obligatory fast is broken only for a physical stopping sign or genuine hardship, then made up later, and a doctor and scholars should be consulted if this recurs; advice includes water in portions from iftar until bedtime, suhoor, quiet activity away from sun and running before iftar, and shorter fasting periods on school, sports and hot days.
text_simplified:
Fasting in children needs close attention: first danger signs, then signs to break the fast, then prevention.

Signs requiring emergency services immediately, at any age and at any point during the fast:
• Fainting or a seizure.
• Confusion, unintelligible speech, or marked drowsiness with difficulty waking.
• Repeated vomiting that prevents drinking.
• Pale, blue or blotchy skin or lips, cold skin, or difficult or very rapid breathing.
• In a child with diabetes: any sign of low blood sugar, such as trembling, sweating or confusion.
What to do: call emergency services and give nothing by mouth until the child is fully conscious. If the child has fainted, lay them on their back and raise their feet until they regain consciousness. For a child with diabetes, follow their doctor's low blood sugar plan.

Signs to break the fast now:
• Severe thirst or a dry mouth and lips.
• Dizziness, blurred vision, paleness or cold sweat.
• Severe headache, persistent abdominal pain or vomiting.
• Unusual tiredness or lethargy, difficulty concentrating or muscle cramps.
• Very little or dark urine, or sunken eyes.
• Before puberty: saying they cannot continue.
What to do: if fully conscious and able to drink safely, the child should break the fast immediately with water and a date or juice, then rest in a cool place. If vomiting, start with small sips and gradually increase. Praise the effort without blame or comparison.

Prevention: water in portions between iftar and suhoor, water-rich foods such as soup, watermelon and cucumber, do not skip suhoor, reduce tea, coffee and salt, and choose quiet activities away from sun and running during fasting hours. Fasting periods should be shorter on school, sports and hot days.

Fasting before puberty is practice, not an obligation. A child must not be forced to fast or fast while ill. After puberty, fasting is obligatory; an obligatory fast is broken only for a physical sign listed here or genuine hardship, and made up later. Seek the details of the rulings from scholars.

When to see a doctor:
• Before any fasting: if the child has diabetes or a chronic illness such as kidney or heart disease, epilepsy or severe anemia, takes medicine regularly during the day, is very thin or has delayed growth, has recently had fever, diarrhea or vomiting, or is preoccupied with weight or severely restricts food.
• Seek urgent medical care now if urine is dark or reduced, the child seems unusually drowsy, dizziness on standing persists, breathing or heart rate is fast, or there are fewer tears. Stop the fast and give water if the child is fully conscious and can drink safely. Do not wait for improvement after breaking the fast before seeking help.
• If breaking the fast for these signs recurs, consult the doctor and scholars.
